The NestedScale object

Source: vignettes/anatomy.Rmd
anatomy.Rmd

This vignette takes one object apart. The example is a small classification of industries by business code, in the style of a statistical classification of activities: sections (C, Manufacturing) hold divisions (C10, Food products), which hold classes (C101). The codes, the names and every number are invented for illustration and reproduce no official classification. The example has every awkward feature: a code reused at two frames, a frame that cross-cuts another, a leaf with no code at one frame, and attributes stored at three different frames.

The cross-cutting frame is size, a grouping of the classes by the typical size of their firms, small or large. Public administration (O84) is not made of firms and has no size, and it is not subdivided, so its only class carries the code of its division.

lt <- data.frame(
  section  = c("C", "C", "C", "C", "C", "D", "D", "D", "O"),
  size     = c("small", "large", "small", "large", "large",
               "large", "small", "small", NA),
  division = c("C10", "C10", "C11", "C24", "C24",
               "D35", "D35", "D35", "O84"),
  class    = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "C241", "C242",
               "D351", "D352", "D353", "O84")
)
at <- data.frame(
  frame     = c("class", "class", "division", "section", "class", "division"),
  member    = c("C101", "C102", "D35", "C", "C241", "D35"),
  attribute = c("wage", "wage", "wage", "wage", "floor_area", "floor_area"),
  kind      = c(rep("property", 4), "factor", "factor"),
  value     = c(30, 28, 45, 32, 60, 20),
  unit_of_measure = c(rep("thousand/employee", 4), "m2/employee",
                      "m2/employee"),
  source    = "example"
)
al <- data.frame(
  frame  = c("class", "division", "class", "division", "division"),
  member = c("C101", "C10", "O84", "O84", "O84"),
  alias  = c("meat", "food", "public admin", "public admin", "government"),
  source = "example"
)
x <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt, frames = c("section", "size", "division", "class"), leaf = "class",
  attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "industries"
)
x
#> NestedScale: industries
#> Frames (4, coarsest first):
#>   - section (3)
#>     - size (2)  [1 member unassigned]
#>       - division (5)
#>         - class (9)
#> Leaves: 9
#> Attributes: wage, floor_area (sources: example) -- 1 at section, 2 at division, 3 at class
#> Aliases: 5 (example)

The object

A NestedScale is an S7 object with eight properties. str() lists them with their size and purpose:

str(x)
#> <NestedScale> industries@92678be1
#> ├─ leaftable    data.frame [9 x 4]            one row per leaf
#> │  ├─ class     leaf column          fixed
#> │  ├─ section   frame                fixed
#> │  ├─ size      frame                fixed
#> │  └─ division  frame                fixed
#> ├─ frames       chr [4]              fixed    section, size, division, class
#> ├─ members      list [4]             derived  from leaftable: section 3, size 2, division 5, class 9
#> ├─ leaf         chr [1]              fixed    class
#> ├─ meta         list [4]             mutable  name, desc, weights, default_weight
#> ├─ attributes   data.frame [6 x 10]  mutable  attach_attributes_scale()
#> ├─ aliases      data.frame [5 x 4]   mutable  attach_aliases_scale()
#> └─ labels       data.frame [0 x 4]   mutable  attach_labels_scale()

The standard S7 tools apply: S7::prop_names(x) gives the names, x@frames or S7::prop(x, "frames") reads one property, and S7::props(x) returns all of them as a list.

S7::prop_names(x)
#> [1] "leaftable"  "frames"     "members"    "leaf"       "meta"      
#> [6] "attributes" "aliases"    "labels"
x@frames
#> [1] "section"  "size"     "division" "class"

The object is a definition: the leaves, the frames that group them, and the weights that say how big each leaf is. It never holds data. Data stays in ordinary tables, and a table is tied to a scale by its code columns; see The data link below.

property type holds
leaftable data.frame one row per leaf: one column per frame, the leaf column, weight columns
frames character the hierarchy, ordered coarsest first
members named list the ordered code vocabulary at each frame
leaf character the name of the leaf column ("leaf" by default)
meta list name, desc, weights, default_weight, and whatever the builder adds
attributes data.frame values keyed by (frame, member): attribute, kind, value, lower, upper, unit_of_measure, source, note
aliases data.frame alternative spellings keyed by (frame, member): alias, source
labels data.frame display names keyed by (frame, member, variant): label

Everything else – parent/child tables, ancestry, shares, resolved attributes – is derived on demand; nothing is cached on the object. The three tables are empty unless the builder fills them; a scale saved by an earlier version, which had no such properties, loads and validates unchanged.

The leaftable 

scale_leaftable(x)
#>   section  size division class
#> 1       C small      C10  C101
#> 2       C large      C10  C102
#> 3       C small      C11  C110
#> 4       C large      C24  C241
#> 5       C large      C24  C242
#> 6       D large      D35  D351
#> 7       D small      D35  D352
#> 8       D small      D35  D353
#> 9       O  <NA>      O84   O84

Each row is one leaf. The leaf column (class here) is unique and complete. Frame columns may hold NA: O84 has no firm size, so it does not participate at the size frame, and na_action= decides what recasts do about it. The leaf column may be the finest frame, as here: the frame column is the leaf column.

Frames, members, ranks 

scale_frames(x)
#> [1] "section"  "size"     "division" "class"
scale_leaf_frame(x)                # the finest frame, or the leaf column
#> [1] "class"
scale_members(x, "division")       # the members at one frame
#> [1] "C10" "C11" "C24" "D35" "O84"
scale_members(x)                   # the leaves
#> [1] "C101" "C102" "C110" "C241" "C242" "D351" "D352" "D353" "O84"
scale_rank(x, "division")
#> [1] 3

Codes are not unique across frames: O84 is a division and a class here. Every function that takes a code therefore takes its frame as well.

Navigation is derived from the leaftable and routed through the leaves, so a frame that cross-cuts another reports overlap rather than invented containment:

scale_nests(x, "division", "class")  # a tree
#> [1] TRUE
scale_nests(x, "size", "division")   # C10 and D35 are small and large
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"offenders")
#> [1] "C10" "D35"
scale_parents(x, "division", "D35", target = "size")
#> [1] "small" "large"
scale_ancestors(x, "class", "D352")
#>      frame member
#> 1  section      D
#> 2     size  small
#> 3 division    D35
scale_descendants(x, "section", "C")
#>       frame member
#> 1      size  small
#> 2      size  large
#> 3  division    C10
#> 4  division    C11
#> 5  division    C24
#> 6     class   C101
#> 7     class   C102
#> 8     class   C110
#> 9     class   C241
#> 10    class   C242
head(scale_ancestry(x), 4)
#>   parent_frame parent child_frame child
#> 1      section      C        size large
#> 2      section      C        size small
#> 3      section      C    division   C10
#> 4      section      C    division   C11

The attribute table

Attributes live in one long table, and a row may sit on any member, not only on a leaf. Here a wage per employee is given for two classes, one division and one section, and a floor area per employee for one class and one division:

scale_attributes(x)
#>      frame member  attribute     kind value lower upper   unit_of_measure
#> 1    class   C101       wage property    30    NA    NA thousand/employee
#> 2    class   C102       wage property    28    NA    NA thousand/employee
#> 3 division    D35       wage property    45    NA    NA thousand/employee
#> 4  section      C       wage property    32    NA    NA thousand/employee
#> 5    class   C241 floor_area   factor    60    NA    NA       m2/employee
#> 6 division    D35 floor_area   factor    20    NA    NA       m2/employee
#>    source note
#> 1 example <NA>
#> 2 example <NA>
#> 3 example <NA>
#> 4 example <NA>
#> 5 example <NA>
#> 6 example <NA>

Reading with a frame resolves one value per member, walking to the nearest coarser frame when a member has none of its own, and says where the value came from:

scale_attributes(x, "wage", frame = "class")[
  c("member", "value", "unit_of_measure", "origin_frame", "origin_member")]
#>   member value   unit_of_measure origin_frame origin_member
#> 1   C101    30 thousand/employee        class          C101
#> 2   C102    28 thousand/employee        class          C102
#> 3   C110    32 thousand/employee      section             C
#> 4   C241    32 thousand/employee      section             C
#> 5   C242    32 thousand/employee      section             C
#> 6   D351    45 thousand/employee     division           D35
#> 7   D352    45 thousand/employee     division           D35
#> 8   D353    45 thousand/employee     division           D35
#> 9    O84    NA              <NA>         <NA>          <NA>

Attributes are not weights. A weight says how big a leaf is and drives aggregation; an attribute is a per-member conversion factor and is consumed only by convert_scale(). The constructor promotes numeric leaftable columns to weights, so a wage must be passed as attributes=, never as a leaftable column. Every attribute name carries a kind: property (an invertible ratio) or factor (one-way).

SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS
#> [1] "property" "factor"

vignette("attributes") has the reasoning and the full account of inheritance, sources and conversion.

The alias table

The members of this scale are codes; the alias table holds the names and spellings by which other tables refer to the same activities.

scale_aliases(x)
#>      frame member        alias  source
#> 1    class   C101         meat example
#> 2 division    C10         food example
#> 3    class    O84 public admin example
#> 4 division    O84 public admin example
#> 5 division    O84   government example
scale_match(x, c("meat", "Public Admin", "C242"))
#>          label frame member    method              candidates
#> 1         meat class   C101     alias                    <NA>
#> 2 Public Admin  <NA>   <NA> ambiguous class/O84; division/O84
#> 3         C242 class   C242     exact                    <NA>

One alias may point at several members (public admin above); matching reports that as ambiguous unless frame= narrows it. Matching is exact and case-insensitive, with no fuzzy stage.

The label table

Labels are display names. A label belongs to a member and to a named variant, so one member may carry a full name, a short one and a translation, while another frame carries none at all and is shown by its codes. A row with member = NA names the frame itself. The divisions get two variants here, a short name and a long one, and the short one is declared the default:

x <- attach_labels_scale(
  x,
  data.frame(
    frame   = "division",
    member  = rep(c("C10", "C24", "O84", NA), 2),
    variant = rep(c("short", "long"), each = 4),
    label   = c("Food", "Metals", "Administration", "Division",
                "Manufacture of food products",
                "Manufacture of basic metals",
                "Public administration", "Division of activity")
  ),
  default = "short"
)
scale_labels(x)
#>      frame member variant                        label
#> 1 division    C10   short                         Food
#> 2 division    C24   short                       Metals
#> 3 division    O84   short               Administration
#> 4 division   <NA>   short                     Division
#> 5 division    C10    long Manufacture of food products
#> 6 division    C24    long  Manufacture of basic metals
#> 7 division    O84    long        Public administration
#> 8 division   <NA>    long         Division of activity
scale_label(x, c("C10", "C11", "O84"), frame = "division")
#> [1] "Food"           "C11"            "Administration"
scale_label(x, c("C10", "C11", "O84"), frame = "division", variant = "long")
#> [1] "Manufacture of food products" "C11"                         
#> [3] "Public administration"
scale_label(x, scale_members(x, "size"), frame = "size")   # no labels: codes
#> [1] "small" "large"

C11 has no label in either variant and is shown by its code. Aliases and labels serve different purposes. An alias is a spelling to be recognised (scale_match()); a label is a name to be shown (scale_label(), join_scale(labels = )).

Weights and meta 

scale_weights(x)                        # none declared here
#> character(0)
S7::prop(x, "meta")[c("name", "desc")]
#> $name
#> [1] "industries"
#> 
#> $desc
#> [1] ""

meta$name is load-bearing: join_scale() prefixes the columns it attaches with "<name>.", scale_map_between() names its label columns after the objects, and write_scale() needs a name for the definition. Further fields passed to the constructor are kept in meta as given.

The data link

A table of data is tied to a scale by its code columns. Unbound, the tie is the column name alone: a column called division is read as codes at the division frame. Two scales can share frame names and codes, so the name does not say which scale the data is on. bind_scale() records it on the column itself, together with the scale’s identity. The link is experimental: it is lost when the column is converted to a factor or a plain character vector, and it may change.

scale_id(x)
#> [1] "industries@92678be1"
d <- data.frame(class = scale_members(x), jobs = seq_along(scale_members(x)))
b <- bind_scale(d, x)
scale_link(b)
#>   column      scale frame                  id
#> 1  class industries class industries@92678be1

scale_id() is the scale’s name plus a hash of its structure – leaf column, frames and memberships. Weights, attributes, aliases and labels do not enter, so enriching a scale does not detach the data bound to it; a subset or a re-grouping is a different scale.

A bound column is still a character vector. It keeps the link through row subsetting, mutate(), grouping, joins and row binding, and the verbs use it: the source frame is taken from the link, the result is bound to the target frame, and data bound to another scale is refused.

register_scale_rule("jobs", "sum")
out <- recast_scale(b, x, target = "division")
scale_link(out)
#>     column      scale    frame                  id
#> 1 division industries division industries@92678be1
clear_scale_rules("jobs")

Unbound data behaves as before, and its results stay unbound. A lazy table (arrow, dtplyr) cannot carry the link in memory; write_scale_dataset() records it in the store and scale_link() reads it back.

What the validator guarantees

scale_from_leaftable() and every operation that rebuilds a scale enforce:

  • the leaf column is present, unique and complete; every frame is a leaftable column and members are exactly its non-NA values, in a stable order;
  • weights are numeric and finite;
  • every attribute and alias row names a (frame, member) that is a member; value is finite; lower <= value <= upper where given; kind is one of SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS and one attribute name has one kind; unit_of_measure and source are non-empty; no duplicate (frame, member, attribute, source) rows and no duplicate alias rows.

The order of frames is a convention, coarsest first; the direction-dependent rules (share, residuals, reconciliation) follow it.

Subsetting keeps the tables consistent: filter_scale() and [ keep the attribute and alias rows of every surviving member at every frame, and prune_scale() keeps the rows at the frames that survive the collapse.

manufacturing <- x["section", "C"]
scale_attributes(manufacturing)[c("frame", "member", "attribute", "value")]
#>     frame member  attribute value
#> 1   class   C101       wage    30
#> 2   class   C102       wage    28
#> 3 section      C       wage    32
#> 4   class   C241 floor_area    60

prune_scale() needs the frames above the new leaf frame to nest, so the cross-cutting size has to go first:

tree <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt[c("section", "division", "class")],
  frames = c("section", "division", "class"),
  leaf = "class", attributes = at, aliases = al, name = "tree"
)
scale_aliases(prune_scale(tree, "division"))
#>      frame member        alias  source
#> 1 division    C10         food example
#> 2 division    O84 public admin example
#> 3 division    O84   government example

Definition files

A scale is stored as a definition, not as an R object: a JSON header with the three tables inline, or, for large scales, a <name>.scale/ bundle directory holding the header and the tables as Arrow IPC or CSV files. The Python binding reads and writes the same files.

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "industries.json")
write_scale(x, path)
cat(head(readLines(path), 12), sep = "\n")
#> {
#>   "schema_version": 2,
#>   "nestedscales": "0.3.0",
#>   "class": "nestedscales::NestedScale",
#>   "name": "industries",
#>   "leaf": "class",
#>   "frames": ["section", "size", "division", "class"],
#>   "members": {
#>     "section": ["C", "D", "O"],
#>     "size": ["small", "large"],
#>     "division": ["C10", "C11", "C24", "D35", "O84"],
#>     "class": ["C101", "C102", "C110", "C241", "C242", "D351", "D352", "D353", "O84"]
back <- read_scale(path)
identical(scale_frames(back), scale_frames(x))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(scale_attributes(back), scale_attributes(x))
#> [1] TRUE

write_scale(format = "yaml") writes the same header as YAML, and read_scale() accepts either. Installed packages register directories of definitions; scale_catalog() lists them and read_scale(id) opens one by its id:

scale_catalog()[c("id", "name", "kind", "frames", "n_leaves", "package")]
#> [1] id       name     kind     frames   n_leaves package 
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

The registry

One package-level registry changes behaviour explicitly. Rules map value-column names to their aggregation rule; there is no fallback, and an unregistered column without rule= is an error:

SCALE_RULES
#> [1] "sum"           "weighted_mean" "mean"          "copy"         
#> [5] "sd"            "share"         "logshare"
register_scale_rule("jobs", "sum")
register_scale_rule("wage", "weighted_mean", weight = "jobs")
get_scale_rule("wage")
#> $rule
#> [1] "weighted_mean"
#> 
#> $weight
#> [1] "jobs"
#> 
#> $scope
#> NULL
list_scale_rules()
#>   param          rule weight scope
#> 1  jobs           sum   <NA>  <NA>
#> 2  wage weighted_mean   jobs  <NA>
clear_scale_rules()

A rule may be scoped to one dimension with scope=, so a jobs column aggregates the same way over industries, regions and months without being registered three times – or differently, when it should.
